items.title: Conjugate function on the circle
items.statement: On trigonometric polynomials on T=R/Z with e_k(x)=e^{2πikx}, define C by (Cf)^hat(k)=-i sgn(k) f^hat(k), sgn(0)=0. Thus C kills constants; extension beyond the polynomial core is not part of the definition.

references.title: Richard S. Laugesen, Harmonic Analysis Lecture Notes
references.locator: Chapter 10, Definition 10.1, printed p. 57

items.strategy: Define a finite coefficient multiplier; check that real polynomials remain real by conjugate symmetry. Fix normalized Haar measure and the 2π negative-forward convention.

items.title: Conjugate Dirichlet kernel and periodic principal value
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. For N≥1 the conjugate partial sum C S_N f is convolution with K_N(t)=2∑_{k=1}^N sin(2πkt)=[cos(πt)-cos((2N+1)πt)]/sin(πt). If f∈L²(T) is C¹ near x, then C f(x)=lim_{ε↓0}∫_{ε<|t|<1/2} f(x-t)cot(πt)dt for almost every such x; finite K_N convolution is not itself a cotangent truncation.

references.title: Richard S. Laugesen, Harmonic Analysis Lecture Notes
references.locator: Chapter 10, Proposition 10.3 and equation (10.3), printed pp. 58–59

items.strategy: Expand the finite multiplier sum and sum the geometric series to obtain K_N. Pair the odd kernel at ±t. Local C¹ regularity makes [f(x-t)-f(x+t)]/sin(πt) integrable; the oscillatory remainder tends to zero by the torus Riemann–Lebesgue lemma after absorbing the half-frequency e^{πit} into the fixed L¹ function supported on 0<t<1/2. Parseval gives L² convergence of C S_N f to the multiplier extension, and an a.e. subsequence identifies that extension with the symmetric principal value. Explicitly retain the finite-sum versus limit distinction.

items.title: Periodic conjugate square identity
items.statement: For every real mean-zero trigonometric polynomial g on T, (Cg)²=g²+2C(g Cg). No assertion for arbitrary Lp inputs is made before bounded extension.

references.title: Loukas Grafakos, Classical Fourier Analysis, third edition
references.locator: §5.1.3, square identity (5.1.23) and Fourier proof, printed pp. 320–321; adapted to zero-mean periodic polynomials

items.strategy: Put F=g+iCg. Its Fourier support consists only of strictly positive modes. Therefore F² has only strictly positive modes; writing F²=u+iv gives C(v)=-u because u and v both have zero mean. Since u=g²-(Cg)² and v=2gCg, rearrange. The zero-mode check is essential on the circle. All calculations are finite and choice-free.

items.title: Marcel Riesz conjugate-function theorem
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. The circle conjugate operator extends uniquely from trigonometric polynomials to a bounded complex-linear C:L^p(T)→L^p(T) for every 1<p<∞, and no compatible strong L¹ or L∞ extension exists. Constants remain in its kernel.

references.title: Richard S. Laugesen, Harmonic Analysis Lecture Notes
references.locator: Chapter 10, Definition 10.1/Lemma 10.2, pp. 57–58; Chapter 12, Corollary 12.2, pp. 70–71 (comparison strong-range result)

references.title: Loukas Grafakos, Classical Fourier Analysis, third edition
references.locator: §5.1.3, Theorem 5.1.7 square-identity/power-interpolation proof, printed pp. 320–322; periodic zero-mode adaptation

items.strategy: For real mean-zero polynomials use the square identity and the L² isometry to inductively bound C in L^{2^m}: if A=||Cg||_{2p}, B=||g||_{2p}, then A²≤B²+2||C||_{p→p}AB. Remove means at cost ≤2 and split complex functions into real and imaginary parts. Extend each power bound from polynomials by Fejér density and Lp completeness; all extensions agree with the L² multiplier on overlaps. Restrict this common operator to finite simple classes and apply the published Riesz–Thorin theorem between adjacent finite powers for every p≥2. For 1<p<2, periodic Lp duality and the L² skew identity give the bound and extension. For the upper endpoint compute the periodic conjugate of an arc indicator as π^{-1}log|sin(πx)/sin(π(x-a))|, unbounded near endpoints; a hypothetical bounded L¹ extension, paired with L∞ test functions using skewness and elementary norming, would force an L∞ bound, contradiction. The latter endpoint argument does not use the later generic weak (1,1) theorem. To rule out a bounded L∞ extension of the polynomial core, approximate the arc indicator by its Fejér means: they are trigonometric polynomials of sup norm at most one and converge in L² to the indicator; a uniform L∞ bound on their conjugates would pass through the L² limit and contradict the logarithmic arc transform.

items.title: Uniform Lp bounds for periodic Fourier partial sums
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. For every 1<p<∞, sup_N ||S_N||_{L^p(T)→L^p(T)}<∞.

references.title: Richard S. Laugesen, Harmonic Analysis Lecture Notes
references.locator: Chapter 9, formula (9.1) and Theorem 9.5 setup, printed pp. 55–56

items.strategy: Define P_+f=(f+iCf)/2+(∫f)/2. Its multiplier is 1 for k≥0 and 0 for k<0; Hölder bounds the mean and Marcel Riesz bounds C. For M_jf=e_j f, verify coefficientwise S_N=M_{-N}P_+M_N-M_{N+1}P_+M_{-(N+1)}. Each modulation is an Lp isometry. This yields the N-independent bound 2||P_+||.

items.title: Periodic Fourier partial sums converge in the strict Lp range
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. S_N f→f in L^p(T) for every f∈L^p(T) and every 1<p<∞. At p=1 and p=∞ this universal norm convergence fails; ||S_N|| grows at least as the Lebesgue constants.

references.title: Richard S. Laugesen, Harmonic Analysis Lecture Notes
references.locator: Chapter 9, Examples 9.3–9.4 and Theorem 9.5, printed pp. 55–56

items.strategy: Fejér convergence supplies dense trigonometric polynomials for finite p. Every S_N fixes a given polynomial once N exceeds its degree; uniform Lp operator bounds then yield convergence. At p=∞ choose the bounded sign of D_N(-t) and evaluate S_Nf at 0 to get ||S_N||∞≥||D_N||₁. At p=1 test S_N on F_M (norm one) and let M→∞; for fixed N, its Fourier coefficients converge to those of D_N, so ||S_N||₁≥||D_N||₁. The published logarithmic lower bound makes both operator families unbounded. Since L¹ and L∞ are Banach under Countable Choice, sequential uniform boundedness implies some input lacks norm convergence at each endpoint. This does not claim divergence for every endpoint input.

items.title: Truncated line Hilbert transform and principal value
items.statement: For 1≤p<∞ and f∈L^p(R), H_εf(x)=π^{-1}∫_{|x-y|>ε} f(y)/(x-y)dy is absolutely defined for every ε>0 and every x. H_pv f(x)=lim_{ε↓0}H_εf(x) only where that limit exists; no general almost-everywhere existence or Lp bound is built into the definition.

references.title: Loukas Grafakos, Classical Fourier Analysis, third edition
references.locator: §5.1.1, Definition 5.1.1 and Remark 5.1.2, printed pp. 314–315

references.title: Richard S. Laugesen, Harmonic Analysis Lecture Notes
references.locator: Chapter 20, Proposition 20.2, printed pp. 114–115

items.strategy: Use Hölder for the tail |x-y|≥ε when p>1, and the ε^{-1} bound when p=1; the representative dependence is null for each fixed x. Distinguish the pointwise partial domain from the later L² multiplier extension, and do not define H on arbitrary L∞ with an uncontrolled tail.

items.title: Sine integral for singular kernel multipliers under Countable Choice
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. The improper integral ∫_0^∞ sin(t)/t dt equals π/2 and its partial integrals are uniformly bounded. Consequently symmetric sine integrals scale to π sgn(x) with a bound independent of the scale; this statement is proved without invoking the published full-AC sine-integral lemma.

references.title: Loukas Grafakos, Classical Fourier Analysis, third edition
references.locator: §5.1.1, equations (5.1.9)–(5.1.12) and uniform sine-integral argument, printed pp. 316–317

references.title: Richard S. Laugesen, Harmonic Analysis Lecture Notes
references.locator: Chapter 20, oscillatory Hilbert kernel calculation (20.2), printed pp. 114–115

items.strategy: Near zero use |sin t|≤|t|. Integration by parts gives the uniform tail bound |∫_A^B sin t/t dt|≤2/A for A≥1. For a>0, absolute Fubini applied to sin t/t=∫_0^1 cos(st)ds yields ∫_0^∞e^{-at}sin t/t dt=arctan(1/a); the tail bound is uniform in a, so pass a↓0 then A→∞. Substitute t↦|x|t for the sign formula. Only the Countable Choice measure/integration convention is used; no full AC supplier is consumed.

items.title: Hilbert principal-value kernel has signum multiplier
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice and the e^{-2πixξ} Fourier convention. On Schwartz functions the principal value exists pointwise, defines the tempered convolution Hf=(pv 1/(πx))*f, and its Fourier transform is -i sgn(ξ) f-hat(ξ).

references.title: Loukas Grafakos, Classical Fourier Analysis, third edition
Richard S. Laugesen, Harmonic Analysis Lecture Notes
references.locator: Chapter 20, Proposition 20.2, printed pp. 114–115

items.strategy: Define W by pairing a Schwartz test with its odd-kernel cancellation on |x|<1 and its integrable tail. This is tempered. Truncate symmetrically in x and at reciprocal large radius; Fubini on finite annuli gives a sine-integral multiplier. The local sine lemma provides a uniform bound and the limit -i sgn ξ; dominated convergence against a Schwartz test yields F(W)=-i sgn ξ in S′. The published tempered-convolution theorem then gives the claimed transform. For each Schwartz f, subtract f(x) on |y|<1 to show the pointwise PV exists and equals W*f.

items.title: Line Hilbert transform is an L² isometry and squares to minus identity
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. The Schwartz Hilbert transform extends uniquely to L²(R), satisfies ||Hf||₂=||f||₂ and H²f=-f for every f∈L²(R). The singleton ξ=0 has no L² zero-mode exception.

references.title: Loukas Grafakos, Classical Fourier Analysis, third edition
Richard S. Laugesen, Harmonic Analysis Lecture Notes
references.locator: Chapter 20, Definition 20.1 and following identities, printed pp. 113–114

items.strategy: Use the exact L² multiplier extension. Since |sgn ξ|=1 off the null singleton, Plancherel gives isometry. The squared multiplier (-i sgn ξ)²=-1 almost everywhere, hence H²=-I on all L². Separate this from the periodic operator, which kills constants.

items.title: Hilbert transform is skew adjoint on complex L²
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice and the first-variable-linear pairing <f,g>=∫f overline(g). Then <Hf,g>=-<f,Hg> for all f,g∈L²(R).

references.title: Loukas Grafakos, Classical Fourier Analysis, third edition
references.locator: §5.1.1, adjoint computation following equation (5.1.15), printed p. 317

references.title: Richard S. Laugesen, Harmonic Analysis Lecture Notes
references.locator: Chapter 20, Definition 20.1 and adjoint identity, printed p. 114

items.strategy: Transport the pairing through the unitary Fourier transform and conjugate the multiplier: overline(-i sgn ξ)=+i sgn ξ=-(-i sgn ξ). The equality extends from Schwartz functions to L² by continuity; state the pairing convention.

items.title: Riesz transforms on Euclidean L²
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice, n≥1 and 1≤j≤n. Define R_j on L²(R^n) by multiplier m_j(ξ)=-i ξ_j/|ξ| for ξ≠0 and m_j(0)=0. Set c_n=Γ((n+1)/2)/π^{(n+1)/2} and K_j(x)=c_n x_j/|x|^{n+1} off 0. The following kernel lemma proves that K_j gives the principal-value formula on Schwartz functions; the definition itself does not assert pointwise limits for all L² inputs.

references.title: Loukas Grafakos, Classical Fourier Analysis, third edition
references.locator: §5.1.4, Definition 5.1.13 and Proposition 5.1.14, printed pp. 324–326

references.title: Richard S. Laugesen, Harmonic Analysis Lecture Notes
references.locator: Chapter 20, Definition 20.1 and Proposition 20.3, printed pp. 113–116

items.strategy: Bound |m_j|≤1 and apply the published L² multiplier theorem; Γ is positive and finite at (n+1)/2. Fix the kernel normalization and origin convention. At n=1, c_1=1/π; comparison with the line Hilbert transform is made in the later example.

items.title: Riesz multiplier equals the principal-value kernel on Schwartz functions
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. For f∈S(R^n), the limit lim_{ε↓0}∫_{|y|>ε} K_j(y)f(x-y)dy exists for every x and gives a continuous representative of the L² multiplier class R_j f, with K_j from the Riesz definition and the 2π Fourier convention.

references.title: Loukas Grafakos, Classical Fourier Analysis, third edition
references.locator: §5.1.4, Proposition 5.1.14 and Lemma 5.1.15, printed pp. 325–327

references.title: Richard S. Laugesen, Harmonic Analysis Lecture Notes
references.locator: Chapter 20, Proposition 20.3 and Lemma 20.4, printed pp. 115–119

items.strategy: Odd spherical cancellation gives convergence at every x after subtracting f(x) near zero; the Schwartz tail is absolutely integrable. The same local domination proves continuity in x. Define the kernel distribution by this cancellation. Fourier-transform finite annuli ε<|y|<1/ε, use polar coordinates, and apply the local uniform sine-integral bound to pass under the spherical integral and Schwartz test. Rotational symmetry makes ∫_{S^{n-1}}sgn(ξ·ω)ω_jdσ=A_n ξ_j/|ξ|, A_n=∫|ω_1|dσ=2π^{(n-1)/2}/Γ((n+1)/2); prove the latter by computing ∫_{B_n}|x_1| twice: polar coordinates give A_n/(n+1), while slices x_1=t and the (n−1)-ball volume give 2V_{n−1}/(n+1); use the published V_{n−1} formula for n≥2 and treat n=1 separately. Thus c_n(π/2)A_n=1 and the transform is -iξ_j/|ξ|. The tempered-convolution law and injectivity of Fourier identify the PV representative with the L² class R_j f. Do not assert a.e. PV convergence on general L² or Lp here.

items.title: Riesz transforms are L² contractions and their squares sum to minus identity
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. Each ||R_j f||₂≤||f||₂ on L²(R^n), and ∑_{j=1}^n R_j²f=-f for every f∈L²(R^n).

references.title: Loukas Grafakos, Classical Fourier Analysis, third edition
references.locator: §5.1.4, Proposition 5.1.16, printed p. 327

references.title: Richard S. Laugesen, Harmonic Analysis Lecture Notes
references.locator: Chapter 20, formulas following Definition 20.1, printed p. 114

items.strategy: Use |ξ_j|/|ξ|≤1 for the contraction. Away from the null origin, ∑_j(-iξ_j/|ξ|)²=-1; apply Plancherel and finite sum. No special constant mode exists in Euclidean L².

items.title: Riesz kernel size, difference and cancellation estimates
items.statement: For n≥1, K_j(x)=c_n x_j/|x|^{n+1} obeys |K_j(x)|≤c_n|x|^{-n}, |K_j(x-h)-K_j(x)|≤C_n|h||x|^{-n-1} when |h|≤|x|/2, and ∫_{S^{n-1}}K_j(rω)dσ(ω)=0 for every r>0. Thus the raw estimates needed by the later singular-integral page hold.

references.title: Loukas Grafakos, Classical Fourier Analysis, third edition
references.locator: §5.1.4, kernel in Definition 5.1.13 and proof of Proposition 5.1.14, printed pp. 324–327

items.strategy: The size estimate uses |x_j|≤|x|. Differentiate x_j|x|^{-n-1}: each partial derivative is bounded by (n+2)|x|^{-n-1}; integrate along x-th for |h|≤|x|/2, where the radius stays ≥|x|/2. Oddness under ω↦-ω makes each spherical integral zero. For n=1 take the two-point sphere. Avoid invoking the later Calderón–Zygmund kernel definition.

items.title: Endpoint map for Hilbert and Riesz transforms
items.statement: The present page proves the periodic conjugate strict Lp range and Euclidean L² facts. The later Calderón–Zygmund page treats weak L¹, real-line/Riesz strict-range Lp and a.e. truncation claims; later real Hardy and BMO pages treat their respective endpoints. The interval examples below refute strong L¹ and L∞ mapping but do not refute weak (1,1) or BMO bounds.

references.title: Richard S. Laugesen, Harmonic Analysis Lecture Notes
references.locator: Chapters 12 and 20, printed pp. 67–71 and 113–119

references.title: Loukas Grafakos, Classical Fourier Analysis, third edition
references.locator: §5.1.3, Remark 5.1.9, printed p. 322

items.strategy: Orientation only. Never use a later result as a premise here. Refer to later planned pages by page title in prose, without unresolved item wikilinks or forward_refs until their item inventories enter the plan. Keep circle/line zero modes and transform-versus-partial-sum endpoint failures separate.

items.title: Hilbert transform of an interval indicator
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. For f=1_(0,1), the symmetric principal value exists for x∉{0,1} and Hf(x)=π^{-1}log|x/(x-1)|. The formula represents the L² multiplier extension almost everywhere.

references.title: Loukas Grafakos, Classical Fourier Analysis, third edition
references.locator: §5.1.1, Example 5.1.3 and equation (5.1.7), printed pp. 315–316

items.strategy: Integrate 1/(x-y) separately in x<0, 0<x<1 and x>1, showing exact cancellation of the two log ε terms in the interior. Mollify the compactly supported indicator with a positive unit-mass smooth bump. The approximants converge in L², so their Hilbert transforms converge in L². At each x outside {0,1}, choose a neighborhood on which the indicator is constant; for sufficiently small mollifier scales the approximants have that same constant there. The local principal-value contributions cancel, while L¹ convergence controls the nonsingular complement pointwise. Thus their Hilbert transforms converge pointwise to the logarithmic principal value. L² uniqueness identifies the multiplier class. Values at the endpoints are immaterial.

items.title: Hilbert transform is not strong type (1,1)
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. The interval indicator belongs to L¹(R), but its Hilbert transform π^{-1}log|x/(x-1)| is not integrable, since it has a nonintegrable 1/|x| tail. Therefore the Schwartz-core transform has no bounded L¹→L¹ extension compatible with the L² transform.

references.title: Loukas Grafakos, Classical Fourier Analysis, third edition

items.strategy: For |x| large, log|x/(x-1)|=-log(1-1/x)=1/x+O(x^{-2}), so its absolute integral diverges. Positive smooth mollifications fε of the interval indicator converge in both L¹ and L². If H had a bounded L¹ extension from the Schwartz core, Hfε would converge in L¹; the L² isometry gives convergence of the same sequence in L² to the logarithmic class. Convergence in measure on every bounded interval identifies the L¹ and L² limits, contradicting nonintegrability of that class. This does not dispute weak (1,1).

items.title: Hilbert transform does not map L∞ to L∞
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. The bounded interval indicator is in L∞(R)∩L²(R), but its compatible Hilbert transform π^{-1}log|x/(x-1)| is essentially unbounded near 0 and 1. There is no bounded L∞ action agreeing with the L² transform on the intersection.

references.title: Loukas Grafakos, Classical Fourier Analysis, third edition

items.strategy: As x→0 or x→1 through positive-measure intervals, the logarithm has arbitrarily large magnitude. Mollify the indicator by a nonnegative unit-mass Schwartz bump: fε stays bounded by one and converges in L². A bounded L∞ extension on the Schwartz core would bound all Hfε uniformly in L∞, while L² continuity makes Hfε converge in L² to the unbounded logarithmic class; an almost-everywhere subsequence would make that class essentially bounded, contradiction. This does not rule out a BMO-valued endpoint.

items.title: Hilbert transform of the line Poisson kernel
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. For a>0, P_a(x)=a/[π(a²+x²)] has Fourier transform e^{-2πa|ξ|}; its Hilbert transform is Q_a(x)=x/[π(a²+x²)], the conjugate Poisson kernel. The identity holds pointwise and in L².

references.title: Loukas Grafakos, Classical Fourier Analysis, third edition
references.locator: §5.1.1, Hilbert signum multiplier, printed pp. 316–317

items.strategy: Multiply the published Poisson transform by -i sgn ξ and invert the two half-line exponential integrals: ∫_0∞e^{-2πaξ}sin(2πxξ)dξ=x/[2π(a²+x²)]. Their signed difference gives Q_a. Both sides lie in L² and are continuous, so Fourier uniqueness upgrades the a.e. identity to pointwise. Note this is the line, not the periodic Poisson kernel.

items.title: Finite sum of Riesz squares in L²
items.statement: Assume Countable Choice. For n≥1 and f∈L²(R^n), the finite sum ∑_{j=1}^n R_j²f=-f. At n=1 this is H²=-I; the assigned value m_j(0)=0 has no effect on L².

references.title: Loukas Grafakos, Classical Fourier Analysis, third edition
references.locator: §5.1.4, Proposition 5.1.16, printed p. 327

references.title: Richard S. Laugesen, Harmonic Analysis Lecture Notes
references.locator: Chapter 20, identities after Definition 20.1, printed p. 114

items.strategy: Write the finite multiplier sum at ξ≠0, equal to -∑ξ_j²/|ξ|²=-1, and use Plancherel. For n=1 identify R_1 with H by the common signum multiplier. Explicitly note that the null singleton does not create a constant-function exception on Euclidean L².
